solutions.check: 30 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 29 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Loud is -not this

parts.note: the clue asks for the word that is the opposite of loud: a sound that is barely audible

explanation.surface: A riddling statement about what a loud noise is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Something barely audible is the opposite of a loud sound, so 'loud' is what it is not.

clue.text: New friend. (and more) for Miranda

indicators.note: something new is freshly made, so the letters of the next words are made over into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Miranda gains a new friend who becomes more than that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges FRIEND and AND. In Shakespeare's The Tempest, Ferdinand is the young prince who becomes Miranda's new friend and then her betrothed, which is the 'and more'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferdinand is the prince in The Tempest who falls in love with Miranda, so he is far more than a friend to her.

clue.text: In leading three of diamonds for this rubber?

indicators.note: the leading three letters are the first three of the following word, taken from its front

explanation.surface: A card player wonders whether diamonds lead in this rubber of bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading three of' takes DIA from 'diamonds'. 'Rubber' suggests a game of bridge, chiming with diamonds, but it is the material: India rubber is the old name for natural rubber, so this answer plus 'rubber' names it.
explanation.definitionFit: India rubber is the traditional name for natural rubber and erasers, so this word is the kind that precedes 'rubber'.

clue.text: Vehicle overturns another on hill

indicators.note: something overturned is turned upside down, so in a down clue the word is read backwards

parts.note: another vehicle is a cart, following on from 'Vehicle'
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A vehicle tips over another one on a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturns' reverses CART to TRAC. 'another' means another vehicle, picking up the definition word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tractor is a farm vehicle used for hauling ploughs and trailers.

clue.text: 17th century play, or preparation for one

explanation.surface: A seventeenth-century drama, or getting ready to stage one.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rehearsal (1671) is a satirical comedy by George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, mocking heroic drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rehearsal is a Restoration comedy by Buckingham; a run-through before a performance is the practice for any play.

clue.text: More revolutionary — after rising, likewise

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read from the bottom up, and likewise says it reads the same that way

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Someone more revolutionary stays the same after an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a palindrome: read upwards ('after rising') it is 'likewise', the same word. 'Red' is the colour of revolutionaries, so redder is more revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Red is the traditional colour of left-wing revolution, so a comparative of red describes someone more revolutionary.

clue.text: How to surround border? Right — plant it

indicators.note: the word 'How' is told to surround, so it is split around the following letters

parts.note: taken as written
an edge is a border or boundary

explanation.surface: A gardener asks how to enclose a border, and is told to plant something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to surround' puts EDGE and R inside HOW. 'How to surround border?' reads as a gardening question, and the answer is the planted thing that would do it.
explanation.definitionFit: A row of shrubs is planted to form a field boundary, so it is something you plant.

clue.text: Carry out no aerial manoeuvre without a wing control

indicators.note: a manoeuvre is a movement or rearrangement, so the letters of 'no aerial' are moved about, with the a after 'without' left out of them

explanation.surface: A pilot is told to perform no aerial manoeuvre without a control on the wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manoeuvre' rearranges NO AERIAL, and 'without a' says one A is taken from those eight letters, leaving seven. 'Carry out' joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An aileron is the hinged flap on an aircraft's wing that controls roll.

clue.text: See about part of speech — I'm upset note

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the first word's letters go round the others

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so these two pieces are read backwards

parts.note: a verb is one of the parts of speech
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone is told to look at a fragment of a speech that upsets them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns VERB IM into MIBREV, and 'about' puts SEE round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A semibreve is the whole note in music, lasting four crotchet beats.

clue.text: Big drink's right in the middle

indicators.note: the letter for right is put in the middle of the drink instead of its end

parts.note: lager is a drink, a light beer

explanation.surface: A big drink sits right in the middle of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the middle' moves the R of LAGER from the end to the centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Large and big are synonyms, both meaning of great size.

clue.text: Caught thus, holding all the diamonds?

definitions.text: Caught thus, holding all the diamonds?

parts.words: Caught thus, holding all the diamonds?
parts.note: a card player with every diamond holds a hand of red cards, and a thief caught in the act is caught this way

explanation.surface: A card player is caught with every diamond in the pack.
explanation.walkthrough: Diamonds are red cards, so a hand of them is a 'red hand'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being caught in the act of wrongdoing is described with this idiom, from blood on the hands.

clue.text: Less convincing work by Debussy

explanation.surface: A piece by Debussy that is less persuasive than his others.
explanation.walkthrough: La Mer is Debussy's orchestral work about the sea; 'lamer' is also the comparative of lame, as in a lame excuse.
explanation.definitionFit: A lame excuse is unconvincing, so a lamer one is less so; La Mer is Debussy's symphonic sketches of the sea.

clue.text: Maid of Pskov's alternative is a dreadful fellow

explanation.surface: An opera's other name belongs to a fearsome man.
explanation.walkthrough: Rimsky-Korsakov's opera The Maid of Pskov is also known by the name of the Tsar who appears in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rimsky-Korsakov's opera The Maid of Pskov has this tsar's name as its alternative title; the sixteenth-century tsar Ivan IV was notoriously cruel.

clue.text: Provide last six of eleven in Manchester sports ground

indicators.note: only the final six letters of the eleven-letter name are kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: Old Trafford, an eleven-letter name, is the Manchester ground for football and cricket

explanation.surface: Supplying the last six players of a team at a Manchester ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eleven' suggests a team, but it counts the letters of OLD TRAFFORD, Manchester United's and Lancashire's ground; 'last six of' keeps the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To afford can mean to give or supply, as in a view that affords pleasure.

clue.text: Note clue about girl's apparent" - - worth

parts.note: fa is the fourth note in the tonic sol-fa scale

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word 'clue' wraps round the name

parts.note: taken as written
Eva is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A clue about a girl hints at her apparent value.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts EVA inside CLUE after its C. The surface reads as a note commenting on a woman, but each word is a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The value printed on a coin or banknote is what it seems to be worth, as opposed to its real value.

clue.text: Tree seen in end of crescent moon's light

parts.note: the pointed tips of a crescent moon are called its horns
a beam is a ray of light

explanation.surface: A tree is glimpsed by the light of a crescent moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of' looks like a call for a last letter, but the tips of a crescent moon are its horns.
explanation.definitionFit: The hornbeam is a hardwood tree of the birch family, common in English hedging.

clue.text: Assess. Stevenson's travelling - -companion?

annotationWithheld.why: clue held as 'Assess. Stevenson's travelling - -companion?' is garbled: MODESTINE is Stevenson's donkey in Travels with a Donkey, but the opening 'Assess.' cannot be repaired with confidence (possibly 'Ass, ...' or 'Ass is ...') and no scan or search gives the printed text

clue.text: Shaw's extra character a comic I strip hero

explanation.surface: A playwright's extra character turns out to be a comic-book hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's play Man and Superman is built on the idea of a man beyond man, the 'extra' character; 'extra' also hints at super-.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's play Man and Superman puts forward the idea of the Übermensch; the caped Krypton-born figure is DC Comics' hero.

clue.text: Proper way to break our codes

indicators.note: breaking codes suggests cracking them, here smashing the letters into a new order

explanation.surface: The correct way to crack our secret ciphers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proper way' wants to be a single idea, but 'Proper' is the definition and 'way to break' points at a rearrangement of OUR CODES.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorous behaviour is seemly and in good taste, which is what proper conduct is.

clue.text: Becomes exhausted, and gets dismissed

explanation.surface: A batsman tires and then loses his wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman is run out when the fielders break the wicket before he completes a run.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplies that are used up have been used to the end; a cricketer caught short of the crease is dismissed in this way.

clue.text: Escort at less than a shilling once

parts.note: ten pence in old money, written 10d, was less than the twelve pence of a shilling

explanation.surface: Escorting someone at a cost of under a shilling in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money had 12 pence (d) to the shilling, so TEN D (tenpence) was less than a shilling.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend someone can mean to accompany or wait on them, as an escort does.

clue.text: Give this a go, having trouble after start of storm

definitions.text: Give this a go, having trouble after start of storm

indicators.note: after says the next piece follows the storm's first letter

parts.note: to give something a go is to try it

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Sailors are urged to try something when a storm brings difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a trysail is a small strong sail set in stormy weather, so you try it when a storm causes trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A trysail is a small fore-and-aft sail hoisted in heavy weather, the one to raise when a gale troubles a ship.

clue.text: An academic is killed while I hunting

parts.note: a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A university lecturer dies in a hunting accident.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the beautiful youth beloved of Aphrodite was gored to death by a boar while hunting.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the handsome youth loved by Aphrodite was killed by a wild boar on a hunt.

clue.text: Twice send evil, say, possibly in this form

definitions.text: Twice send evil, say, possibly in this form

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be arranged in another way
twice means the word that follows is used two times over

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A suggestion that sending evil twice over might take this shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' doubles SEND, and 'possibly' rearranges SENDSEND with EVIL and SAY into the fifteen letters. The whole clue also defines: the evils sent are these sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath and sloth are the deadly vices of Christian teaching, evil in a listed form.

clue.text: European with small house in London?

explanation.surface: A European who owns a little house in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Swiss Cottage is a district of north London named after a chalet-style inn, so this word plus a small house gives a London place.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Switzerland is a European; a cottage is a small house, and Swiss Cottage is a London district.

clue.text: Epic story of one Irish house's overthrow

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: overthrown in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: the Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament

explanation.surface: The epic tale of one Irish parliament's downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overthrow' turns DAIL upside down to LIAD. The surface fits too: Homer's epic tells of the war that ended in Troy's overthrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's Iliad is the ancient Greek epic poem of the Trojan War.

clue.text: Dwelling — single one now pointless

indicators.note: the compass points N, S, E and W are all removed from the three words

explanation.surface: A house that was once one-of-a-kind is now without purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointless' looks like 'useless', but it strips every compass point (S, N, E, W) from SINGLE ONE NOW, leaving I, G, L, O, O.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a dome-shaped dwelling built from blocks of snow by Inuit peoples.

clue.text: Chap, possibly Latin one, in Dickens

definitions.text: Chap, possibly Latin one, in Dickens

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be arranged in another way

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A man in Dickens who may be of Latin origin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges LATIN to TALIN. Mr Mantalini, the foppish husband of a dressmaker in Nicholas Nickleby, is indeed a chap with an Italianate, Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Mantalini is the affected, extravagant husband of Madame Mantalini in Dickens's novel Nicholas Nickleby.

clue.text: Swindles about small apples

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first word's letters enclose the second's

parts.note: a sting is a slang word for a swindle or confidence trick
wee is Scottish for small

explanation.surface: Con tricks involving small apples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts WEE inside STINGS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweeting is an old name for a sweet-flavoured variety of apple.

clue.text: Place in bank (for otter, maybe)

explanation.surface: An otter's home tucked into a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' looks like a riverbank in the surface, but in the first sense it is a bank for money: to deposit funds there. An otter's den, like a beaver's, can be called this.
explanation.definitionFit: To lodge money is to deposit it with a bank; an animal's den such as a beaver's or otter's home is also named so.
